title: Modules: Versioning & Workspaces
summary: A **Go module** is a versioned collection of packages with a `go.mod` file at its root. Modules give Go reproducible builds through **semantic versioning**, **minimal version selection**, and a checksum database — and **workspaces** (`go.work`) let you develop several interdependent modules together without publishing or editing each `go.mod`.

subtopics.title: go.mod and go.sum
subtopics.explanation: go.mod declares the module path, the Go version, and the dependency requirements (`require`). go.sum records cryptographic checksums of every dependency (and its go.mod) so the toolchain can verify that what you download matches what was recorded — protecting against tampering. Commit both files.
subtopics.example:
module github.com/me/app

go 1.22

require github.com/x/y v1.4.0

subtopics.title: Semantic versioning (semver)
subtopics.explanation: Module versions are tags of the form vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. MAJOR bumps signal breaking changes, MINOR adds backward-compatible features, PATCH fixes bugs. Go takes semver literally: a v2+ major version is treated as a different module with a different import path, which keeps incompatible versions from colliding in one build.

subtopics.title: Minimal Version Selection (MVS)
subtopics.explanation: Unlike resolvers that pick the newest matching version, Go picks the MINIMUM version that satisfies all requirements — the highest version among those explicitly required, but no higher. This makes builds reproducible and upgrades intentional: you only get a newer version when some require line actually asks for it.
subtopics.example: if A needs C v1.2 and B needs C v1.5, the build uses C v1.5 (the max of the required minimums)

subtopics.title: The /v2+ import path rule
subtopics.explanation: For major version 2 and above, the major version must appear in BOTH the module path in go.mod (`module github.com/me/lib/v2`) and in every import path (`import "github.com/me/lib/v2"`). This 'semantic import versioning' lets v1 and v2 of the same library coexist in one build, since they're distinct import paths.

subtopics.title: require, replace & exclude
subtopics.explanation: `require` lists dependencies and their minimum versions. `replace` redirects a module path to a local directory or a fork (great for local dev or patched deps). `exclude` forbids a specific bad version. replace is for development convenience; prefer real versions for published modules.

subtopics.title: Workspaces (go.work)
subtopics.explanation: A go.work file lists multiple local modules with `use`, so the toolchain resolves imports between them from your working tree instead of published versions — no replace directives, no committing temporary edits. Ideal when you're editing a library and an app that consumes it at the same time. go.work is typically NOT committed.

foundations.overview: Before modules, Go relied on GOPATH and your dependencies were whatever happened to be checked out — builds weren't reproducible. Modules fixed that: a module is a unit of versioned code identified by a path, pinned by go.mod, and verified by go.sum. Go's version resolution is deliberately conservative (it picks the minimum versions that satisfy everyone), and major versions are encoded into import paths so incompatible versions can coexist. Workspaces add a developer-friendly layer for editing several modules at once.
foundations.formalDefinition: A module is a tree of Go packages rooted at a directory containing a go.mod file, identified by a module path and released as semantically-versioned units; dependency selection uses Minimal Version Selection over the transitive require graph, and a workspace (go.work) overlays multiple local modules for unified resolution.
foundations.whyItMatters: Reproducible, verifiable builds are foundational to supply-chain security and team velocity. Understanding semver, MVS, the /v2 rule, and replace vs workspaces is what separates engineers who can confidently upgrade dependencies and ship libraries from those who fight 'it works on my machine' and import-path errors.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of go.mod as a shopping list with minimum acceptable versions, go.sum as the tamper-evident receipt, and MVS as a thrifty shopper who buys the lowest version that still satisfies every recipe. A workspace is like temporarily wiring several of your own kitchens together so they share ingredients straight off the counter instead of from the store.
foundations.runtimePerspective: Modules are entirely a build-time concept — the compiled binary contains no module metadata beyond what you embed (e.g. via runtime/debug.ReadBuildInfo, which does expose the module graph for diagnostics). Version selection, downloading (via the module proxy), and checksum verification all happen before compilation.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Every modern Go repo has a go.mod. Companies run a private module proxy (GOPROXY) and verify against GOSUMDB; monorepos and multi-module repos use go.work for local development; library authors cut /v2 paths for breaking releases.
foundations.businessImpact: Reproducible builds and checksum verification reduce supply-chain risk and 'works on my machine' incidents, while MVS makes upgrades auditable. Workspaces speed up multi-module development, cutting iteration time for platform teams.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Modules make dependency upgrades explicit and reviewable (a go.mod diff), and the /v2 rule prevents diamond-dependency conflicts. The cost is learning semver discipline and the occasional confusion around replace, go.sum, and major-version paths.
foundations.performanceImpact: No runtime impact. Build-time cost is dominated by downloading and verifying modules, which a local/proxy cache (GOMODCACHE, GOPROXY) makes fast and reproducible.
commonUseCases: Publishing a breaking release as a /v2 module
Local development across an app and its library via go.work
Redirecting a dependency to a fork or local path with replace
Verifying supply-chain integrity through go.sum and GOSUMDB

commonMisconceptions.myth: Go picks the newest available version of each dependency.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Go uses Minimal Version Selection: the highest version any require line demands, but never newer than required — newest-available is not chosen automatically.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can bump to v2 just by tagging v2.0.0.
commonMisconceptions.reality: For v2+, the major version must be in the module path AND every import path (semantic import versioning); a bare tag without the /v2 path breaks consumers.
go.work only overlays resolution across local modules for development; each module still has its own go.mod, and go.work is usually not committed.

visualExplorer.title: How a build resolves and verifies dependencies
visualExplorer.caption: From go.mod to a verified, reproducible build.

config.intro: When you run `go build`, the module system does this:

steps.name: Read go.mod
steps.detail: The toolchain reads your module path, Go version, and require list — the minimum versions you depend on.

steps.name: Build the version graph
steps.detail: It follows each dependency's own go.mod transitively to learn what THEY require.

steps.name: Apply MVS
steps.detail: For each module it selects the maximum of all required minimum versions — reproducible, and never newer than asked.

steps.name: Fetch via GOPROXY
steps.detail: Missing modules are downloaded from the module proxy into the local cache (GOMODCACHE).

steps.name: Verify with go.sum
steps.detail: Each download's checksum is compared against go.sum (and GOSUMDB); a mismatch fails the build, catching tampering.

interactiveExamples.title: A go.mod and the commands that shape it
interactiveExamples.explanation: go.mod is mostly machine-managed: `go get` adds/upgrades requires, `go mod tidy` prunes unused ones and fills in go.sum. Read it as a manifest of minimum versions, not exact pins.

code.code:
# Start a module
go mod init github.com/me/app

# Add a dependency at a specific version
go get github.com/google/uuid@v1.6.0

# Remove unused deps and complete go.sum
go mod tidy

# Show the final selected versions (after MVS)
go list -m all | head -n 3
code.expectedOutput:
go: creating new go.mod: module github.com/me/app
go: added github.com/google/uuid v1.6.0
github.com/me/app
github.com/google/uuid v1.6.0

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: wire up a workspace for local dev
interactiveExamples.explanation: You're editing ./lib and want ./app to use your in-progress changes without publishing or adding a replace directive. Fill in the go work commands. Reveal the solution to see the canonical flow.

code.code:
# app imports github.com/me/lib, which lives at ./lib (unpublished edits)
# TODO: create a workspace so `go build ./app` uses ./lib from disk

# 1) initialize the workspace including both modules
# 2) build the app and confirm it sees local lib
echo 'fill in the go work commands'
code.solution:
# Create a go.work that overlays both local modules.
# `use` tells the toolchain to resolve these module paths from disk.
go work init ./app ./lib

# Now imports of github.com/me/lib in ./app resolve to ./lib directly —
# no replace directive, no committing temporary go.mod edits.
go build ./app/...

# go.work is for local development; add it to .gitignore (usually not committed).
# To add another module later:  go work use ./tools
code.expectedOutput: (go.work created listing ./app and ./lib; go build resolves lib from disk)

checkpoints.prompt: Module A requires C v1.2.0; module B requires C v1.5.0. Under Minimal Version Selection, which version of C does the build use?
options: It errors on a version conflict
checkpoints.explanation: MVS selects the maximum of all required minimum versions, so v1.5.0 wins — it satisfies both A (>=1.2) and B (>=1.5). It does NOT jump to the newest published version, and it does not error: both requirements are compatible.

checkpoints.prompt: A library released v2.0.0 with this go.mod, and consumers can't import the new features. What's wrong?
options: The module path is missing the /v2 suffix required for major version 2
checkpoints.explanation: For v2 and above, semantic import versioning requires the major version in the module path: `module github.com/me/lib/v2`. Without it, the toolchain treats the v2.x.x tags as not belonging to this module path, so consumers can't import the v2 API.

checkpoints.prompt: What does this print, given a clean module that only imports the standard library?
checkpoints.code:
// after: go mod init example.com/m
// running: go list -m
checkpoints.explanation: `go list -m` with no arguments prints the main module's path — example.com/m — even with zero external dependencies. The module always exists once go.mod is created.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the go.mod directive that redirects a dependency to a local checkout for development.
checkpoints.explanation: `replace github.com/x/y => ../y` points the dependency at a local directory. `use` belongs in go.work, `exclude` blocks a version (no `=>`), and `redirect` isn't a go.mod keyword.

codeLab.title: Parse and compare semantic versions
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Less(a, b string) bool` that reports whether semver string a is strictly less than b. Versions look like "v1.4.0" (always three numeric components, with a leading 'v'). Compare MAJOR, then MINOR, then PATCH numerically. This mirrors how MVS orders versions.
hints: Strip the leading 'v' with strings.TrimPrefix, then strings.Split on '.'.
Compare major first; only fall through to minor/patch when the higher component is equal.
Equal versions are NOT strictly less, so return false when all three match.

debuggingLab.title: go get can't find the v2 features
debuggingLab.symptom: After upgrading a dependency to its v2 release, `go get github.com/acme/lib@v2.1.0` works but `import "github.com/acme/lib"` still gives the old API, and importing v2 symbols fails to compile.

brokenCode.caption: The import path has no /v2 suffix.

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Under semantic import versioning, a v2+ module lives at a path ending in /v2. The path github.com/acme/lib refers to the v1 module; the v2 code is a *different* import path, github.com/acme/lib/v2. Importing the bare path keeps resolving v1, so the v2 symbols are undefined. This is by design — it lets v1 and v2 coexist in one build.
commonMistakes: Assuming a v2 tag changes the import path automatically.
Editing go.mod's require version without changing the import path.
Forgetting that v1 and v2 are distinct modules that can both be present.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Update the import path (and the corresponding require line) to include the /v2 suffix.

theory.question: Explain Minimal Version Selection and why Go chose it over picking the newest version.
theory.directAnswer: MVS builds the transitive requirement graph and, for each dependency, selects the maximum of the minimum versions that any module requires — never anything newer than something explicitly asks for. Go chose it because it makes builds reproducible and upgrades intentional: adding a dependency can't silently pull in a brand-new, untested version of something else; you only move forward when a require line says so.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A deterministic algorithm that selects the lowest versions consistent with all stated requirements.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To guarantee reproducible builds and avoid the unpredictability of 'always newest' resolvers.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: It walks each dependency's go.mod, collects required minimums, and for every module takes the highest of those minimums as the selected version.

theory.whyImportant: It's a defining, frequently-tested property of Go modules and explains why `go get -u` (explicit upgrade) is separate from a normal build.
theory.realWorldExample: Two libraries require C v1.2 and v1.5; the build uses v1.5 and stays there until you explicitly upgrade, so CI today builds exactly what it built last week.

followUps.question: How do you intentionally upgrade everything to latest?
followUps.answer: Run `go get -u ./...` (or `go get -u=patch` for patch-only), which rewrites require lines to newer versions; MVS then selects those.

followUps.question: What guarantees the downloaded code matches what was selected?
followUps.answer: go.sum checksums, verified against the checksum database (GOSUMDB), fail the build on any mismatch.

theory.question: What is semantic import versioning and what changes when a library releases v2?
theory.directAnswer: Semantic import versioning encodes a module's MAJOR version (for v2 and above) directly into its import path and module path — e.g. github.com/me/lib/v2. When you cut v2, you must add the /v2 suffix to the module line in go.mod and to every import of the package. This treats v2 as a distinct module so it can coexist with v1 in the same build, avoiding diamond-dependency conflicts.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A rule that the major version (>=2) is part of the module/import path.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Because v2 may break v1's API, and two incompatible versions must be importable simultaneously in a large dependency graph.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The toolchain treats github.com/me/lib and github.com/me/lib/v2 as separate modules, each with its own selected version.

theory.whyImportant: Misunderstanding it causes broken v2 releases and 'undefined symbol' errors; it's a classic senior-Go interview probe.
theory.realWorldExample: A widely-used JSON or routing library bumps to v2 with a new API; consumers import .../v2 while transitive deps may still pull v1 — both build cleanly.

followUps.question: Does v0 or v1 need a suffix?
followUps.answer: No — v0 and v1 use the bare module path; only v2+ requires the major version in the path.

scenario.question: Your team develops an app and a shared library in two repos. Mid-feature you need to test app changes against unreleased library changes. Compare using a replace directive vs a go.work workspace.
scenario.directAnswer: Both make the app resolve the library from a local path. A `replace github.com/me/lib => ../lib` lives in the app's go.mod — it works but it's easy to accidentally commit, polluting published builds. A go.work file with `use ./app` and `use ./lib` does the same overlay without touching either go.mod, and is conventionally not committed, so there's no risk of shipping a local path. For multi-module local development, workspaces are the cleaner, lower-risk choice.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two mechanisms for resolving a dependency from local disk during development.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To iterate on a library and its consumer together before publishing a version.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: replace rewrites resolution inside go.mod; go.work overlays multiple modules' resolution externally, leaving each go.mod pristine.

scenario.whyImportant: Committing a replace to ../lib breaks everyone else's build — a common real-world incident that workspaces prevent.
scenario.realWorldExample: A platform team edits a shared SDK and the service using it simultaneously via go.work, then publishes the SDK version and removes nothing from go.mod.

followUps.question: When is replace still the right tool?
followUps.answer: For a long-lived redirect that SHOULD be committed — e.g. pointing a dependency at a maintained fork or pinning a security patch fork.

coding.question: Implement `SelectMVS(reqs map[string]string) map[string]string` that, given each module's required minimum version, returns the version MVS would select per module. Versions are semver strings like "v1.5.0"; the map may list the same module multiple times only if you merge inputs — here assume one entry per module but the function should be the merge primitive used across modules.
coding.thoughtProcess: MVS selects, per module, the maximum of all required minimum versions. The primitive is: given two requirements for the same module, keep the higher version. I'll implement that merge over a list of (module, version) requirements so multiple inputs collapse to the per-module max — exactly the MVS rule.
coding.lineByLine: parse splits a semver into a [major,minor,patch] array. higher compares two versions component-by-component and returns the larger string. MergeMVS walks every requirement and, for each module, keeps the higher of the current selection and the new requirement — which is precisely MVS's 'maximum of the minimums.' The result maps each module to its selected version.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) over the number of requirements (constant-size version parsing).
coding.spaceComplexity: O(m) for the selection map over m distinct modules.

followUps.question: How does real MVS get the requirements?
followUps.answer: By transitively reading each module's go.mod require lines, building the full version graph, then applying this max-of-minimums rule per module.

followUps.question: Why isn't 'pick the newest published version' equivalent?
followUps.answer: Newest-published is non-reproducible and can pull untested versions; MVS only advances when a require line demands it, keeping builds stable.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Keep one go.mod per module and a tidy require list; isolate breaking changes behind /v2 import paths so consumers migrate on their own schedule. For multi-module repos, use a committed structure plus an uncommitted go.work for local development.
productionDeepDive.performance: Module resolution is build-time only; speed it with a warm module cache (GOMODCACHE) and a fast/internal GOPROXY. `go mod download` in CI pre-warms the cache so builds don't hit the network repeatedly.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Not a runtime concern, but the toolchain downloads and verifies modules in parallel; a reliable proxy avoids flaky concurrent fetches against upstream VCS.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Commit go.mod and go.sum for reproducible builds, and run `go mod verify` plus checksum-DB validation in CI so a tampered or yanked dependency fails fast rather than shipping silently.
productionDeepDive.observability: Use `go list -m all` to see selected versions, `go mod graph` to inspect the dependency graph, and `go mod why <pkg>` to learn why a dependency is present — essential for auditing and trimming.
productionDeepDive.security: go.sum plus the public checksum database (GOSUMDB) detect dependency tampering; run a private GOPROXY and vet new dependencies (govulncheck) to manage supply-chain risk. Never commit a replace pointing at a local path into release branches.

caseStudies.company: Large Go monorepos (e.g. infra platform teams)
caseStudies.problem: Develop many interdependent modules without constant publish-and-bump cycles.
caseStudies.solution: Adopt go.work to overlay local modules during development; publish versions only when stable.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: go.work eases local iteration but must not be committed, and CI still builds against published versions to stay honest.
caseStudies.lessons: Separate local-dev resolution (workspaces) from release resolution (versioned go.mod).

caseStudies.problem: Ship a breaking API without breaking existing v1 users.
caseStudies.solution: Use semantic import versioning: module path and imports gain a /v2 suffix so v1 and v2 coexist.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: More ceremony when releasing majors, but zero diamond-dependency conflicts downstream.
caseStudies.lessons: Encode major versions in the import path; never reuse the v1 path for breaking changes.

keyTakeaways: A module is versioned code rooted at go.mod; go.sum checksums make builds verifiable and reproducible — commit both.
Minimal Version Selection picks the maximum of all required minimum versions, so upgrades are intentional, not automatic.
Semantic import versioning puts the major version (v2+) in the module AND import paths, letting incompatible versions coexist.
Use replace for committed redirects (forks/patches) and go.work workspaces for uncommitted, multi-module local development.
